### 🔍 Search Terms

"anonymous symbol properties"
"anonymous unique symbol"
"inline unique symbol"
"unique symbol property key"
"computed property unique symbol"
"symbol branding"

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

Allow `unique symbol` keys to be declared inline at the property declaration site.

### 📃 Motivating Example

**Current code:**
```ts
declare const brand: unique symbol;
type UserId = string & { readonly [brand]: "UserId" };
```

**Proposed code:**
```ts
type UserId = string & { readonly [brand: unique symbol]: "UserId" };
```

Each inline declaration would create a fresh symbol identity, equivalent to declaring a separate `unique symbol` and using it as the computed property key.
   
This is useful when a `unique symbol` property key is needed only once and does not need to be referenced independently. Common examples include phantom properties used for branded or refined types.

### 💻 Use Cases

1. What do you want to use this for?
   Declaring single-use `unique symbol` property keys inline, particularly for phantom properties used by branded or refined types.

2. What shortcomings exist with current approaches?
   The current approach requires introducing a value-level declaration solely to provide a unique identity for a type-level property key. For single-use symbol keys, this creates an otherwise unnecessary binding in the surrounding scope.

3. What workarounds are you using in the meantime?
   Declaring a separate `unique symbol` value and using it as a computed property key.
issues.title: Anonymous Symbol Properties

### 🔎 Search Terms

memory, oom, resolveObjectTypeMembers, getReducedType

### 🙁 Actual behavior

we have a ~37k file TS program at work and checking it on 7.0 needs ~13 GiB of heap single threaded (~16 GiB peak), and about double that with the default 4 checkers. people keep running out of memory, esp with the editor open too

i profiled it and there are two spots where the checker builds a ton of stuff it never uses:

- looking up one property on an instantiated class/interface (`expect(x).toBe`, `arr.map` etc) instantiates every member of the type plus everything it inherits. on our program thats ~15.7M member symbols and only ~3M of them ever get used. `isWeakType`, `getSingleSignature` and friends also build the whole table just to count stuff
- `getReducedType` builds the combined property for every name in an intersection just to check if it reduces to `never`. only a handful of names can actually do that (shared across constituents with a literal type, or private)

### 🙂 Expected behavior

only build what's needed. i have changes for both that give the same output as main. full go test suite passes (also with multiple checkers and `-race`) and i added tests for the edge cases i hit along the way

typescript-benchmarking tsc scenarios with both changes, 4 checkers, median of 3:

| | heap | peak rss | check time |
|---|---|---|---|
| vscode | 6.22 → 5.65 GiB (−9%) | 9.75 → 8.97 GiB (−8%) | same |
| mui-docs | 4.75 → 2.72 GiB (−43%) | 6.80 → 4.03 GiB (−41%) | 5.89 → 3.86s (−35%) |
| xstate-main | 0.55 → 0.49 GiB (−10%) | 0.67 → 0.61 GiB (−8%) | same |
| webpack | 0.94 → 0.84 GiB (−11%) | 1.15 → 1.00 GiB (−13%) | 0.51 → 0.48s (−6%) |
| Compiler | −4% | −6% | same |
| Compiler-Unions | −8% | −2% | same |

single threaded looks about the same (vscode −8% heap, mui-docs −35%). the intersection change is basically all of the mui-docs win and the member change is the ~8-10% on everything else. on our own program heap goes 13.1 → 10.4 GiB

output matched main on every run except TS6059 on mui-docs, but that one flakes on main too (#64477)

opened #64475 (members) and #64476 (intersections) as drafts. #64475 overlaps with #64372, and a lot of the complexity in it is there to keep the half built members behavior that #64372 removes. so if that lands first ill rebase and it should get a lot simpler

### Additional information about the issue

`--generateTrace` couldnt handle a program this size (the types dump went past 160 GB before i killed it) so i found these with go heap profiles and some counters hacked into the checker

fwiw i used claude code for a lot of the digging and the code. ive reviewed it and ill be the one following up on review

### 🔍 Search Terms

- protected alternative
- internal

Related issues:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/18499
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/5228

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

Currently, `protected` causes several issues:
- you can't use duck typing when a class have a `protected` property. You can't implement it, you are required to extend it. 
- `protected` (and `private`) properties often disappear when manipulating types.

I'd like an `internal` modifier that would behave similarly to `readonly`.
It would declare the property is part of the public interface, but you can't access it outside of its methods (a.k.a. functions where the type of `this` is the type of the instance).

### 📃 Motivating Example

Such feature could be used for several usages.

**Having friends**

Currently, TS has no friend, even though this seems to be a frequently requested feature:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/7692
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/35554

An `internal` modifier would be a cleaner way to have friends:
1. you declare a function/class with some internal properties.
2. you can safely cast such object by removing the `internal` modifier with some type manipulations (e.g. with `-internal`).

You can then select exactly which properties are accessibles from friends (which helps respecting encapsulation).

**Implementing classes with internal properties**

Sometimes we want to implement a class instead of extending it. However, this is not possible when using `protected` properties:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/61161

**Defining interfaces with internal properties**

We could also define interfaces with internal properties, e.g. hooks that could be overridden when extending a class implementing the interface, without even requiring to know the class true concrete type.

**Manipulating internal properties**

This would also enable more complex type manipulations, e.g.:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/46802

### 💻 Use Cases

Currently, there are several workarounds.

**Cast**

```ts
const internal = target as FooInternals;
```

Can be dangerous. A "type map" can be used to make the cast slightly more secure, but this is still unsafe.

**Public properties**

Making the properties public solves most of the issue, however, this makes properties publicly accessible, loosing some protections.

**Symbols**

We can hide the internal type behind a symbol.

```ts
class Foo {
      [SYMBOL] = this as InternalFoo;
      // or
       [SYMBOL] = { ... }
}
```

However, this is not ideal when manipulating classes in mixins (attributes aren't accessible from the prototype, and we can't really manipulate the constructor).

**Hooks in the constructor**

In some cases, you can give hooks in the base class constructor instead of overriding protected methods.

```ts
class Foo {
      [HOOKS]: XX; // not in the FooClass interface.

      constructor(hooks) {
             this[HOOKS] = hooks;
      }
}
```

But same as previously, this is not ideal when manipulating classes in mixins.

**Static properties**

Another way is to declare static instance methods that can be redefined:
```ts
class X {
      static onChange = () => {};
      foo() {
            this.constructor.onChange.call(this); // not type safe.
      }
}
```

However this is not truly type safe:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/3841

**Alternative suggestion :**

This issue could also be solved by specifying a public and an internal type for the same property:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/37487
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/54829

The usage could then be something like `foo: $PUB_TYPE @internally=$INTERNAL_TYPE`, e.g.:
- `foo: never @internally=number`.
- `foo: readonly number @internally=number`.
- `foo: X @internally=XInternals`.

However this would require bigger changes to TS.
issues.title: An `internal` property modifier as an alternative to `protected`

### 🔍 Search Terms

content mapper, contentMappers, extensionless import, extension-less import, custom file extension, extraExtensions, resolveHiddenExtensions, moduleSuffixes, bundler module resolution

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

Let the extensions registered in `contentMappers` take part in extensionless module lookup, after every built-in extension (`.ts`, `.tsx`, `.d.ts`, `.js`, `.jsx`), in the resolution modes that already add extensions (`bundler`, `node10`, and the CommonJS side of `node16`/`nodenext`).

```ts
// tsconfig.json: "contentMappers": [{ "package": "identity-foo-mapper", "extensions": [".foo"] }]
import { value } from "./card"; // today: TS2307; suggested: resolves to card.foo when no card.ts, card.tsx, card.d.ts, card.js or card.jsx exists
```

The mapper process plays no part in resolution. The resolver already reads the registered extension list to resolve fully specified imports such as `./card.foo` (the `extraExtensions` branch of `tryAddingExtensions`); this uses the same list in the extensionless branch. #64546 asked for this as a bug and is working as intended; this is the suggestion form.

A prototype against main at [`b85298b`](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/b85298b6a81f772d080b0455de0ca9d744cd6fd6/tsc/internal/module/resolver.go#L1518-L1545):

```diff
--- a/tsc/internal/module/resolver.go
+++ b/tsc/internal/module/resolver.go
@@ -1542,6 +1542,16 @@ func (r *resolutionState) tryAddingExtensions(extensionless string, extensions e
 				return resolved
 			}
 		}
+		if originalExtension == "" && extensions&(extensionsTypeScript|extensionsDeclaration) != 0 && !r.isConfigLookup {
+			// Content-mapper extensions take part in extensionless lookup after every built-in
+			// candidate, so an existing .ts, .tsx, .d.ts, .js or .jsx file always wins.
+			for _, extension := range r.resolver.extraExtensions {
+				if resolved := r.tryExtension(extension, extensionless, false); !resolved.shouldContinueSearching() {
+					resolved.resolvedUsingExtraExtensions = true
+					return resolved
+				}
+			}
+		}
 		return continueSearching()
 	default:
 		if slices.Contains(r.resolver.extraExtensions, originalExtension) {
```

Results with the identity `.foo` mapper from #64546's reproduction, main vs. a local build of main with the prototype above:

| Case | main | prototype |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `./card` from a `.ts` file | TS2307 | resolves to `card.foo` |
| `./card` from a mapped `.foo` file | TS2307 | resolves to `card.foo` |
| `./card` with `moduleSuffixes: [".web", ""]` | TS2307 | resolves to `card.foo`: the compiler option puts the suffix after `.foo` (#64548). With the `moduleSuffixes` list on the `contentMappers` entry from #64560, resolves to `card.web.foo` |
| `./widgets` with `widgets/index.foo` | TS2307 | resolves to `widgets/index.foo` |
| `./card` with `card.ts` and `card.foo` | `card.ts` | `card.ts` |
| `./card` with `card.d.ts` and `card.foo` | `card.d.ts` | `card.d.ts` |
| `./card` with `card/index.ts` and `card.foo` | `card/index.ts` | `card.foo` (see below) |
| `./card` under `nodenext` ESM | TS2834 | TS2834 |

`go test ./internal/module/... ./internal/modulespecifiers/... ./internal/contentmapper/...` passes with the prototype; I have not run the full baseline suite.

Open questions:

1. **Opt-in or always on.** The one resolution that changes is a registered file next to a same-named directory: `./card` picks `card.foo` over `card/index.ts`, a file before a directory, as a bundler configured with `.foo` does. Content mappers are not in a stable release yet, so no shipped project depends on the old result. If it should stay opt-in, a flag on the `contentMappers` entry or in the mapper's manifest would do it; #64560 already puts a `moduleSuffixes` list on the entry.
2. **Declaration emit.** The declaration for `card.foo` is emitted as `card.d.foo.ts`, so an emitted `.d.ts` that keeps `./card` does not resolve for consumers without the mapper. Projects with `noEmit` are unaffected. This overlaps with #64053 / #64120.
3. **Editors.** I have not checked whether the language server picks up a newly created `card.foo` for an import that already failed to resolve.

### 📃 Motivating Example

Tools that type-check their own file formats through Volar on TypeScript 5.x/6.x resolve `import Greeting from "./Greeting"` to `Greeting.<ext>` with Volar's `resolveHiddenExtensions`. Content mappers are how those tools move to TypeScript 7, and today that move means adding the extension to every such import, including imports from `.ts` and `.tsx` files:

```ts
// app.ts in an Ember app, with Greeting.gts next to it
import Greeting from "./Greeting"; // Glint on TypeScript 6: Greeting.gts. A content mapper on TypeScript 7: TS2307.
```

Glint added `resolveHiddenExtensions` so that Ember apps can import `.gts` components without the extension (volarjs/volar.js#190, typed-ember/glint#806). Other language tools that set it today, or whose users want it:

- [Glint](https://github.com/typed-ember/glint/blob/main/packages/ember-tsc/src/volar/ember-language-plugin.ts) (`.gts`, `.gjs`)
- [ArkTS](https://github.com/ohosvscode/arkTS/blob/next/packages/language-plugin/src/language-plugin.ts) (`.ets`)
- [Imba](https://github.com/imba/imba/blob/main/packages/imba-language-core/src/languagePlugin.ts) (`.imba`)
- [Octane](https://github.com/octanejs/octane/blob/main/packages/octane/src/compiler/typescript.js) (`.tsrx`)
- [Ripple](https://github.com/Ripple-TS/ripple) (`.tsrx`)

### 💻 Use Cases

1. **What do you want to use this for?** TSRX type-checks `.tsrx` files through a content mapper on TypeScript 7 (tsrx-org/tsrx#135). Bundlers configured with the extension resolve `./Card` to `Card.tsrx`, as esbuild does for `.foo` in #64546's reproduction. Cross-platform projects import platform variants (`Card.web.tsrx`, `Card.ios.tsrx`) as `./Card` through `moduleSuffixes`, which tsrx-org/tsrx#971 enables on TypeScript 5.x/6.x through Volar. On TypeScript 7 that also needs #64560, because the compiler option puts the suffix after a registered extension (#64548).
2. **What shortcomings exist with current approaches?** Only fully specified imports resolve. A mapper cannot help: it is asked for a file's content after resolution has picked the file, and it cannot register `.ts` or `.tsx`, so it never sees the `.ts` files that import mapped files. Every such import has to carry the extension, which neither the bundler nor these tools require today.
3. **What workarounds are you using in the meantime?** Explicit extensions (`./Card.tsrx`). A second one works on TypeScript 7 but needs a generator kept in sync with the file system: one re-export shim per mapped file in a hidden folder, merged in with `rootDirs`, the way SvelteKit resolves `./$types`.

The prototype and results were prepared with Claude Code; every result above was run locally.
issues.title: Content mappers: let registered extensions take part in extensionless module lookup

issues.body:
VS Code's built-in TypeScript extension lets other extensions send requests to its server with the `typescript.tsserverRequest` command: built-in requests from a short list, and any request whose name starts with `_` (a tsserver plugin can register those). Extensions for content-mapped languages need this, because several commands accept only TypeScript and JavaScript files.

The TypeScript 7 extension has no equivalent. The object its `activate` returns offers `registerContentMappers`, `onLanguageServerInitialized` and `initializeAPIConnection` (the native API, not the language server's requests), and no command forwards a request to `tsc --lsp`.

### Use cases

From TSRX (`.tsrx` files, served through a content mapper):

| Feature | VS Code's TypeScript (5.9 or 6) | TypeScript 7 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Go to Source Definition | TSRX's command sends `findSourceDefinition` through `typescript.tsserverRequest` (as a `_tsrx:` request that its tsserver plugin registers), and it works in `.tsrx` files | `tsc --lsp` answers `custom/textDocument/sourceDefinition` for content-mapped files, but the extension's command accepts only TypeScript and JavaScript language IDs (#64576), and no other extension can send the request |
| Find File References | same approach possible | not implemented yet (#63806); once it is, TSRX needs a way to ask for it on a `.tsrx` file |

With a way to send requests, an extension could offer these features for its own files without waiting for each command to accept content-mapped languages.

### Suggestion

A way for an extension to send a request to `tsc --lsp`, for example:

- `sendRequest(method, params, token)` on the API object, or
- a `typescript.native-preview.sendRequest` command, like `typescript.tsserverRequest`.

It could be limited to documents of the content mappers that the calling extension registered with `registerContentMappers`, or to `custom/*` methods.

Found while adding TypeScript 7 support for `.tsrx` files (https://github.com/tsrx-org/tsrx/issues/136).
issues.title: TypeScript 7 VS Code extension: let other extensions send requests to tsc --lsp, like typescript.tsserverRequest

### 🔍 Search Terms

extraFileExtensions
ScriptKind.Unknown
getDefaultProjectForFile
companion files
cold start project
openProjects




### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

Something like content mappers for registering extra extensions as included in the project but without the requirement of actually doing content mapping

### 📃 Motivating Example

We're currently prototyping the new Angular Language Service against TS-Go (`tsgo --lsp` with the API session pipe). In our setup, our extension manages a separate language server to handle Angular-specific template features, and uses TS-Go as the backend semantic and type-checking engine.

Because we manage our own compiler instance per `tsconfig.json`, we need to know which project owns a file when it's opened. We're running into a cold-start discovery problem when a user opens an external template first (e.g. `app.component.html`): `getDefaultProjectForFile` returns nothing because TS doesn't recognize `.html` as belonging to any configured project. Since Angular hasn't compiled yet, we don't know the TS ↔ HTML association either, so we don't know which tsconfig to load.

To work around this today, we do a "fake open dance" where we guess a sibling `app.component.ts` file, send a synthetic `didOpen` to TS-Go just to spin up the project and discover the tsconfig path, and then boot our compiler.

Content Mappers don't really fit here because they require transforming foreign files into virtual `.ts` ASTs and generating `.ts` output. For Angular, HTML files are external companion templates—our template type-checking code is generated out-of-band in separate `.ngtypecheck.ts` files. Forcing a Content Mapper onto `.html` files just introduces unwanted `.ts` AST generation and emit overhead.

Previously, `extraFileExtensions` with `ScriptKind.Unknown` kept projects active when matched by `include` globs. Since non-TS extensions in `include` globs are more standard now with content mappers, we're fine requiring `.html` in `include`. A lightweight extension registration (or a no-transform companion mode that lets `include` globs associate `.html` with `ProjectService` without generating virtual `.ts` ASTs) would eliminate the cold-start issue and the fake open workaround.

### 💻 Use Cases

1. What do you want to use this for?
Angular language service

3. What shortcomings exist with current approaches?
Mentioned above

5. What workarounds are you using in the meantime?
attempting to open a ts file with the same name
issues.title: Associate companion files with `ProjectService` without Content Mappers

issues.body:
### 🔍 Search Terms

virtual file
setVirtualFile
RequestFileSystem
openClientFiles
didOpen didClose
temporary file update

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

Add an overlay mechanism over the LSP server interface (`tsgo --lsp`) to push in-memory file contents directly into TS-Go's VFS (for example, a custom notification like `ts/setVirtualFile` with `{ path, content }`, where `null` clears the overlay) without treating the files as client-opened documents.

### 📃 Motivating Example

We're using `tsgo --lsp` (with the API session pipe) as our backend diagnostics and type-checking engine for the Angular Language Service. To type-check templates, Angular generates synthetic in-memory TypeScript files containing Type Check Blocks (like `app.component.ngtypecheck.ts`) that TS-Go needs to type-check alongside user code.

Right now, we feed these into TS-Go by sending synthetic `textDocument/didOpen` and `textDocument/didChange` notifications. While that works, treating these files as client-opened documents pollutes `openClientFiles`, artificially bumps project retention ref-counts in `ProjectService`, and forces us to manage synthetic open/close lifecycle bookkeeping for files that aren't actually open in the editor.

The API client already has some support for layered VFS snapshots (`RequestFileSystem` with `{ kind: "layer" }` and `runWithTemporaryFileUpdate`), but we don't have an equivalent way to push un-opened virtual files over the LSP connection.

An overlay notification over LSP (something like `setVirtualFile(path, content | null)`) would let us push our generated type-check files directly into TS-Go's VFS without `openClientFiles` pollution or open/close bookkeeping.

### 💻 Use Cases

 1. What do you want to use this for?
To feed Angular's generated template type-checking code (`.ngtypecheck.ts` files containing Type Check Blocks) into TS-Go in memory. 

We run `tsgo --lsp` as an out-of-proc semantic and diagnostics engine for both our dev server and our separate Angular Language Server. As users edit templates, we generate and update these synthetic `.ngtypecheck.ts` files so TS-Go can type-check them alongside the user's TypeScript code and answer semantic queries (hover, definition, completions). None of these synthetic files exist on disk, and they change frequently as templates are edited.

2. What shortcomings exist with current approaches?
Over LSP, the only current way to provide in-memory content is via `textDocument/didOpen` and `textDocument/didChange`. Because `didOpen` is built for user-facing editor buffers, using it for internal synthetic files causes a few headaches:
- It registers the files in `openClientFiles`, adding unnecessary tracking overhead for files the user never opened.
- It inflates `ProjectService` retention ref-counts, keeping configured projects alive longer than they should be or creating awkward project lifecycle behavior.
- We have to build our own synthetic `didOpen` / `didClose` bookkeeping layer just to keep TS-Go's internal project state clean.

The API client recently added layered snapshot file systems (`RequestFileSystem` with `{ kind: "layer" }` and `runWithTemporaryFileUpdate`), but that's scoped to immutable snapshots in the Node API client rather than a long-running `tsgo --lsp` server session answering standard LSP requests.

 3. What workarounds are you using in the meantime?
In our language service facade, we currently fake the document lifecycle: we track synthetic version numbers, send `textDocument/didOpen` when generating a TCB, `textDocument/didChange` as the template updates, and send `textDocument/didClose` when components are removed or projects unload. It works functionally, but it's fragile and forces us to manage artificial lifecycle bookkeeping for purely ephemeral compiler artifacts.
issues.title: In-memory virtual file overlay over LSP without faking `didOpen`

"add missing properties", "quick fix", "code action", "TS 7", "native language server"

- This changed between versions 6.0.3 and 7.0.2
- This changed in commit or PR: unknown (likely the codefix hasn't been ported to the native language server)
- This is the behavior in every version I tried, and I reviewed the FAQ for entries about quick fixes and the TS 7 native language server (none found)
- Note: 6.0.3 was tested in the Playground, where "Add missing properties" is offered. The Playground has no TS 7 option, so TS 7.0.2 was tested in VS Code 1.140.0.

### 💻 Code

```ts
type T = { a: number; b: string }
const t: T = {}
```


### 🙁 Actual behavior

Error: `Type '{}' is missing the following properties from type 'T': a, b`
"No quick fixes available" when TypeScript 7 Language Server is enabled

### 🙂 Expected behavior

Error: `Type '{}' is missing the following properties from type 'T': a, b`
Quick Fix "Add missing properties" is offered. After applying:
```ts
type T = { a: number; b: string }
const t: T = {
a: 0,
b: ""
}
```


### Additional information about the issue

The playground link is for TypeScript 6.0.3 as there is no option to use Typescript 7.0 ("Nightly" is v6.0.0-dev.20260416)

issues.body:
### 🔍 Search Terms

infer type generic parameters

Related comment:
- https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/26242#issuecomment-411084229

Did find some issue about "Higher-kinded types", but none on inference.
Do not confuse this issue with the ones asking for an infer in the generic type contraints.

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

Allowing an `infer` keyword when defining a generic type:
```ts
type Y<T extends number> = {};
type X<infer T> = Y<T>;
// equivalent to:
type X<T extends number> = Y<T>
```

The `infer` keyword would tell TS that the contraints (and default value) of `T` should be fetched from the definition of `Y`.

**Possible improvement:**

When we have multiple generic parameters, it could also be nice to be able to do:
```ts
type X<infer ..T> = Y<..T>
```
But IIRC some issues already request features for a `..T`.

**Possible alternative 1:**

Being able to fetch a generic parameter definition from an existing type:
```ts
type Y<T extends number> = {};

type X<T extends Y{T}> = Y<T>;
type X<T extends Y{1}> = Y<T>; // starts at 1 if we want 0 to have a special meaning.
type X<T: Y{1}> = Y<T>;
```

**Possible alternative 2:**

Being able to define generic parameters outside of type definition:
```ts
typeparams P = [
      T extends number,
      U extends string,
];

type Y<..P> = { foo: P.T, faa: P.U };
type X<..P> = Y<..P>;
```

For this one, a current alternative is to use a bag:
```ts
type P = {
      T: number,
      U: string
}

type Y<T extends P> = {foo: T["T"], faa: T["U"]};
type X<T extends P> = Y<T>;
```
However, I'm pretty sure it causes issues when inferring.

### 📃 Motivating Example

When defining generic types from other generic types, we have to copy/paste all the contraints.
This code duplication is a pain, makes the code harder to read, and can be error prône if the contraints change.

```ts
type Y<
                 T extends A<number>,
                 U extends B<any>,
                 V extends C<any>
> = {};

type X<infer T, infer U, infer V> = Y<T, U, V>;
// vs
type X<
                 T extends A<number>,
                 U extends B<any>,
                 V extends C<any>
            > = Y<T, U, V>;
```

### 💻 Use Cases

1. What do you want to use this for?

Easily defining generic types from other generic types.

2. What shortcomings exist with current approaches?

Lot of duplicated contraints.

3. What workarounds are you using in the meantime?

Duplicated contraints.
issues.title: Defining a type with inferred generic parameters

### 🔍 Search Terms

typescript/sync api round trips, getPropertiesOfType per member, bulk symbol documentation, getMembersOfType, api extractor performance, jsii typescript 7, out-of-process checker queries

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

I am an independent contributor experimenting with running jsii (the AWS CDK's multi-language binding generator) on the TypeScript 7 programmatic API. This proposal comes out of that work, and I think it applies to other tools of the same kind.

Tools that extract an API surface from a whole program (jsii, TypeDoc, API Extractor, documentation generators) visit every exported type and, for every member, ask the checker for the member's properties, its declared type, the type that declares it, and its JSDoc. On the out-of-process API each of those questions is one round trip, so the traversal is bounded by the number of round trips rather than by checker work. jsii spends about 33 s traversing aws-cdk-lib and issues about 700k requests in that time; the server spends only about 6 s of it computing types, and the rest goes to waiting for round trips and handling messages.

I propose two additional methods. One returns the JSDoc of many symbols at once. The other returns, for a single type, everything such a traversal needs about its members (symbol, declaring type, kind, JSDoc, declared type) in one round trip. On aws-cdk-lib this brings the request count from 700k down to 300k and the traversal from 33 s to 28 s. Existing methods are unchanged and the new ones return the same handles, so callers can migrate incrementally.

Both methods run against the existing API checker and return the same symbol and type handles the fine-grained methods return; callers rely on handle identity to correlate types across calls, so that is preserved.

`getSymbolDocumentations(symbols[])` returns, per symbol, exactly what `getJsDocTags` and `getDocumentationComment` return. One request per type's member list instead of two per member.

`getMembersOfType(type, filter)` returns the members of a type that satisfy the filter. Each entry carries the member's symbol, the symbol of the type that declares it, its kind (method or constructor parameter property), its JSDoc, and on request its declared type. This is the union of what a member-processing loop asks for individually today.

The filter exists because of a measurement. A first attempt that fetched the declared type of every member and discarded the unwanted ones afterwards was slower than the fine-grained traversal: at aws-cdk-lib scale, private and internal members are the majority, and the cost of materialising types for members the caller throws away cancelled the round-trip savings. To materialise only the types of members that will actually be used, the caller has to tell the server what to drop.

The filter is an options object of independent conditions:

| option | meaning | jsii passes | other tools |
|---|---|---|---|
| `visibility` | visibilities to include; ECMAScript private names count as private | public, protected | a public-API extractor passes public only |
| `kinds` | member kinds to include (property / accessor / method / parameterProperty) | all | a documentation tool that renders accessors separately |
| `excludeJsDocTags` | drop members whose JSDoc carries any of these tags | internal (plus deprecated when stripping) | TypeDoc's `@hidden`, API Extractor's `@internal` / `@alpha` |
| `excludeNamePattern` (RE2) | drop members whose name matches | `^_` | any naming convention |
| `includeInheritedFrom` | which declaring types contribute members | the type's unexported base types | `all` for a flattened view, empty for own members only |
| `includeDeclaredType` | attach the declared type to each member | true | false for a name-only listing |


### 📃 Motivating Example

Request mix for jsii's TypeScript 7 backend over aws-cdk-lib (the snapshot jsii-compiler uses for its benchmark, 20,221 types and 97,071 members): `getJsDocTags` 134k, `getTypeAtLocation` 125k, `getDocumentationComment` 117k, `getTypeOfSymbolAtLocation` 105k, `getTypeFromTypeNode` 47k, `getPropertiesOfType` 23k.

A Go execution trace of the server shows the handler for these per-member methods takes 1.6–5 µs each; the round trip the client observes is 26 µs, and the server spends 24 s of a 45 s run blocked waiting for the next request. The traversal is dominated by the number of messages, not by the checker.

The existing mechanisms do not help this pattern. `batchRequests` cannot bundle a member traversal because its requests depend on each other: the type's property list is needed before the properties' types can be asked for. Client-side caching does not help either: the duplicate rate for documentation reads and `getPropertiesOfType` is 0%, and memoising `getTypeAtLocation` (80% duplicates) removed 113k requests but no measurable wall clock, because repeated requests are cheap on the server and the cost is the message itself.

Results, same fork build, c7i.4xlarge, aws-cdk-lib benchmark, with the sync-channel waiting improvement from the separate proposal enabled, median of 3 runs, `.jsii` output byte-identical between the two paths:

| path | wall | requests | transport wait | bytes sent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fine-grained (today's methods) | 34.5 s | 698k | 8.6 s | 131 MB |
| `getSymbolDocumentations` + `getMembersOfType` | 29.4 s | 304k | 5.4 s | 52 MB |

A current aws-cdk-lib checkout built from source (2 runs): 43.2 / 43.1 s → 37.8 / 38.2 s, requests 783k → 340k, bytes sent 168 MB → 65 MB, server time unchanged (22.1 → 21.5 s).

The implementation, with Go unit tests, is on the fork branch `WinterYukky/TypeScript` `api/coarse-endpoints-generic-filter-1792824451`.


### 💻 Use Cases

1. Tools that extract an API surface from a whole program through the API: jsii (multi-language bindings for the AWS CDK), documentation generators such as TypeDoc, and API extractors.
2. Each member costs several round trips today, and neither `batchRequests` (the requests depend on each other) nor client-side caching (few duplicates) reduces them.
3. None; jsii issues the per-member requests and accepts the round-trip cost.

I used an AI coding assistant while implementing and measuring this change; the issue, the design and the review responses are mine.
issues.title: API: coarse-grained checker queries for tools that extract a whole API surface (`getSymbolDocumentations`, `getMembersOfType`)

### 🔍 Search Terms

[deprecated union literal](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20deprecated%20union%20literal), [`@deprecated` literal type](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20%40deprecated%20literal%20type), [deprecated string literal](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20deprecated%20string%20literal), [jsdoc deprecated union member](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20jsdoc%20deprecated%20union%20member)

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

`@deprecated` on one member of a union of literals doesn't do anything right now. it'd be great if using that value got the same strike-through and suggestion a deprecated property does.

### 📃 Motivating Example

you can deprecate one value of a union, and editors strike it through wherever it's used, the same way they do for a deprecated property.

```ts
type LogLevel = "debug" | "info" | "warn" | /** @deprecated use "warn" */ "warning";

declare function log(level: LogLevel, msg: string): void;

log("warning", "disk almost full");
//  ~~~~~~~~~ 'warning' is deprecated.
```

### 💻 Use Cases

1. library and API authors retiring one accepted value (a renamed option, an old mode) that still works, so callers see it in their editor before it's removed.
2. there's no way to mark it today. dropping the value from the type turns a soft deprecation into a type error on code that still runs.
3. a deprecated overload ahead of the normal one. it only works when the value is passed straight to a function, and each deprecated value needs another overload:

```ts
/** @deprecated use "warn" */
declare function log(level: "warning", msg: string): void;
declare function log(level: LogLevel, msg: string): void;
```
issues.title: Honor @deprecated on a literal member of a union
